Besides using the iPhone 18 Pro, I also did a small experiment at the same time, carried out during the wait for the iPhone Duo to be released.

To get a feel for what it would be like to use the upcoming large screen, I had been occasionally using the iPad mini as a phone replacement. Given that the two have similar screen sizes and shapes, I was hoping this would give me a preview of that feeling…

I’ll be the first to admit that I don’t really need to own an iPad mini. Most of the time I only use it to read library ebooks borrowed through the Libby app, because in the UK there’s no way to read those books on a Kindle. (Don’t get me started on that bizarre omission…)

Looking back at how many ebooks I’ve read, having an extra device dedicated to reading isn’t entirely unreasonable, but I do feel a bit guilty that a device with so many capabilities is playing such a limited role. Still, I’ve finally found at least one temporary new use for it: getting a sense of the experience the iPhone Duo might offer.

As my colleague Ryan Christoffel mentioned earlier, the iPhone Duo’s internal display is a little smaller than the iPad mini’s, but the difference isn’t actually that big.

Because the iPhone Duo has much slimmer bezels, the difference in screen size isn’t as obvious as you might think: iPhone Duo: 7.6-inch display; iPad mini: 8.3-inch display

What I did was install all the same apps as on my iPhone, arranged as similarly as possible, to try to mimic that experience as closely as I could. My iPhone’s Wi-Fi hotspot provided the connectivity I needed, so I could use the iPad in many of the situations where I’d normally reach for my iPhone.

In some ways, the iPad mini experience is actually better than the Duo’s, because it runs iPadOS rather than iOS, which makes multitasking more flexible. I don’t like using windowed mode on such a small screen, though, so I mainly stick to full-screen or split-screen modes, which are actually quite similar to the Duo’s interface.

To make up for the fact that it doesn’t fit in a pocket, I only carry it when I have a backpack with me, which is roughly half the time I’m out.

Of course, the iPad doesn’t support every feature the Duo will have, so it’s only a very rough stand-in for the experience — but it really did give me a good sense of what it would be like to have such a large screen on a phone, and I thoroughly enjoyed the process.

Every time I switch back from the iPad mini to the iPhone 18 Pro, the screen really does look tiny. This little experiment has done absolutely nothing to dampen my anticipation for the upcoming new model.
